<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The \emph{structure function} of $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ is
$h_x(\alpha)=\min\{\log|S| : x\in S\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ C(S)\le\alpha\}$
for $\alpha\ge c\log n$. A model is \emph{sufficient} if
$C(S)+\log|S|\le C(x)+c\log n$, and the \emph{sophistication}
$\mathrm{soph}(x)=\min\{\alpha : h_x(\alpha)+\alpha\le C(x)+c\log n\}$ is the
complexity of a minimal sufficient statistic~\cite{Ko87,GTV,VV04}. The
string is \emph{stochastic} if $\mathrm{soph}(x)=O(\log n)$, and
\emph{antistochastic} if $h_x(\alpha)\approx n-\alpha$ for all
$\alpha<C(x)$~\cite{M15}.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:basic}
For $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ with $C(x)=\kappa$, up to $O(\log n)$:
(i) $h_x(\alpha)\ge\kappa-\alpha$; (ii) $h_x(c\log n)\le n$ and
$h_x(\kappa)=0$; (iii) (\emph{halving law}) $h_x(\alpha)+\alpha$ is
non-increasing. Conversely~\cite{VV04}, every simple function with
(i)--(iii) is the structure function of some $x$ up to $O(\log n)$; such
functions are called \emph{admissible}.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A model $A\ni x$ is \emph{$\varepsilon$-strong} if
$\mathit{CT}(A\mid x)\le\varepsilon$, and
$h^{\mathrm{str}}_{x,\varepsilon}(\alpha)=\min\{\log|A| : x\in A,\
\mathit{CT}(A\mid x)\le\varepsilon,\ C(A)\le\alpha\}$. A string is
\emph{$(\varepsilon,\delta)$-normal} if
$h^{\mathrm{str}}_{x,\varepsilon}(\alpha+\delta)\le h_x(\alpha)+\delta$ for all
$\alpha$, and \emph{strange} if it has no strong minimal sufficient
statistic.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:partition}
If $A\ni x$ is $\varepsilon$-strong, there is a partition $p$ of
$\{0,1\}^n$ with $C(p)\le\varepsilon+O(\log n)$ and a cell
$A_1\ni x$ of $p$ with $A_1\subseteq A$ and
$C(A_1)\le C(A)+\varepsilon+O(\log n)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $r$ be a total program with $r(x)=A$ and $|r|\le\varepsilon$. Group
the strings $x'$ with $x'\in r(x')$ according to the value $r(x')$, and
put every other string in a singleton cell. This partition is
computable from $r$ and $n$, and the cell of $x$ is
$A_1=\{x''\in A : r(x'')=A\}$, computable from $A$, $r$ and $n$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:VV}
If $\mathcal{A}$ is acceptable, $h^{\mathcal{A}}_x$ obeys the halving law, and for every
admissible shape $P$ there is $x$ with $h_x$ and $h^{\mathcal{A}}_x$ both
$C(P)+O(\sqrt{n\log n})$-close to $P$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:galois}
$\mathrm{orb}_G(U)\le p\iff U\le\mathrm{stab}_G(p)$. Hence both maps are monotone,
$U\le\mathrm{stab}_G\mathrm{orb}_G(U)$, $\mathrm{orb}_G\mathrm{stab}_G(p)\le p$, and the \emph{closed
subgroups} ($U=\mathrm{stab}_G\mathrm{orb}_G U$) correspond bijectively and
order-preservingly to the \emph{symmetric partitions}
($p=\mathrm{orb}_G\mathrm{stab}_G p$), which are exactly the orbit partitions of
subgroups of $G$. Denote their lattice by $\mathrm{Par}_G$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If every $U$-orbit lies in a cell of $p$, each cell is a union of
$U$-orbits and is $U$-invariant; conversely, if $U$ preserves every
cell its orbits lie in cells. The rest is the general theory of
Galois connections.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:closed}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
\item $G=\mathrm{Sym}(X)$: every partition is symmetric, and the canonical
certificates are the \emph{Young subgroups} $\prod_{B\in p}\mathrm{Sym}(B)$.
\item $G=S_n$ permuting the coordinates of $\{0,1\}^n$: $\mathrm{orb}(S_n)$ is
the partition into weight classes; subgroups give finer
``combinatorial'' partitions.
\item $G=\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$: symmetric partitions are rigid. If
$W\ne\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is a subspace with $\dim W\ge2$, the partition
$\{W\setminus\{0\}\}\cup\{\text{singletons}\}$ is not symmetric: any
$g$ preserving it fixes every vector outside $W\setminus\{0\}$, these
span $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, so $g=1$. With a canonical complement $D$, the orbit
partition of $\mathrm{GL}(W)\times\{\mathrm{id}_D\}$ is symmetric; its cells
are $\{d\}$ and $d+(W\setminus\{0\})$, $d\in D$. A cell can appear
only together with the other orbits of its certificate.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:canon}
For $U\le G$ with $p=\mathrm{orb}_G(U)$ and a cell $B$ of $p$:
\[
  C(\mathrm{stab}_G p)\le C(p)+O(1)\le C(U)+O(1),\qquad
  C(\mathrm{stab}_G p,B)=C(p,B)\pm O(1).
\]
The canonical certificate is, up to $O(1)$, the cheapest group with the
given orbits, and it costs exactly as much as the hypothesis.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Orbits are computable from generators; $\mathrm{stab}_G(p)$ is computable from
$p$ by search in $G_n$, and $n$ is recoverable from $p$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A set $S\subseteq X$ is \emph{$G$-homogeneous} if $G_{\{S\}}$ acts
transitively on $S$. Let $\mathcal{A}_G$ denote the family of non-empty
$G$-homogeneous subsets of $X$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:cells}
Let $S\subseteq X$ be non-empty.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $S$ is a cell of some partition in $\mathrm{Par}_G$ if and only if
$S\in\mathcal{A}_G$.
\item If $S\in\mathcal{A}_G$, then $p_S=\mathrm{orb}_G(G_{\{S\}})$ is the coarsest
partition in $\mathrm{Par}_G$ having $S$ as a cell: every $p\in\mathrm{Par}_G$ with
$S\in p$ refines $p_S$.
\item If $S\in\mathcal{A}_G$, then $C(p_S,S)=C(S)\pm O(1)$. For every partition
$p$ having $S$ as a cell, $C(S)\le C(p,S)+O(1)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
(i) If $S=U\cdot x$ for some $U\le G$, then $U\le G_{\{S\}}$, so
$G_{\{S\}}$ is transitive on $S$. Conversely, if $G_{\{S\}}$ is
transitive on $S$, then $S$ is one of its orbits, hence a cell of
$p_S$, which is symmetric by Proposition~\ref{prop:galois}.
(ii) If $p\in\mathrm{Par}_G$ and $S\in p$, then $\mathrm{stab}_G(p)\le G_{\{S\}}$, so
$p=\mathrm{orb}_G\mathrm{stab}_G(p)\le\mathrm{orb}_G(G_{\{S\}})=p_S$ because $\mathrm{orb}_G$ is
monotone.
(iii) $G_{\{S\}}$, and hence $p_S$, is computable from $S$ by search in
$G_n$, and $n$ is recoverable from $S$. Conversely $S$ is computable
from $(p,S)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:cells}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
\item $G=\mathrm{Sym}(X)$: every non-empty set is homogeneous, and $p_S$ is
$\{S,X\setminus S\}$ (or $\{X\}$ if $S=X$).
\item $G=\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$: a homogeneous set containing $0$ is $\{0\}$, since
$0$ is fixed. Theorem~\ref{thm:homog} identifies the others.
\item $G=\mathrm{GL}(3,2)$: $79$ of the $255$ non-empty subsets of $\mathbb{F}_2^3$ are
homogeneous, distributed by size $1,\dots,8$ as
$8,21,35,7,0,7,1,0$. Every pair and every triple of nonzero vectors is
homogeneous, and no $5$-set is. Only $100$ of the $4140$ partitions of
$\mathbb{F}_2^3$ are symmetric, but $695$ have every cell homogeneous. See Figure~\ref{fig:cells}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{P}$ assign to each $n$ a family of partitions of $\{0,1\}^n$. A
\emph{$\mathcal{P}$-model} for $x$ is a pair $(p,B)$ with $p\in\mathcal{P}$ and
$x\in B\in p$. Define
\begin{align*}
h^{\mathcal{P}}_x(\alpha)&=\min\{\log|B| : (p,B)\ \mathcal{P}\text{-model},\ C(p,B)\le\alpha\},\\
h^{\mathcal{P}}_{x,\varepsilon}(\alpha)&=\min\{\log|B| : (p,B)\ \mathcal{P}\text{-model},\
C(p)\le\varepsilon,\ C(p,B)\le\alpha\},\\
\mathrm{soph}^{\mathcal{P}}(x)&=\min\{\alpha : h^{\mathcal{P}}_x(\alpha)+\alpha\le C(x)+c\log n\}.
\end{align*}
$C(p)$ is the cost of the \emph{hypothesis} and $C(B\mid p)$ that of
the \emph{cell}; $C(p,B)=C(p)+C(B\mid p)$ up to $O(\log n)$. For an
ambient group $G$ we write $h^G_x$, $h^G_{x,\varepsilon}$ and
$\mathrm{soph}^G$ for $\mathcal{P}=\mathrm{Par}_G$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:basicP}
Up to $O(1)$ shifts:
(i) $h_x\le h^{\mathcal{P}}_x\le h^{\mathcal{P}}_{x,\varepsilon}$, and $\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{P}'$
implies $h^{\mathcal{P}'}_x\le h^{\mathcal{P}}_x$;
(ii) every cell of a partition of complexity at most $\varepsilon$ is
$(\varepsilon+O(1))$-strong, so
$h^{\mathrm{str}}_{x,\varepsilon+c}\le h^{\mathcal{P}}_{x,\varepsilon}$;
(iii) $\mathrm{soph}(x)\le\mathrm{soph}^{\mathcal{P}}(x)$ up to $O(\log n)$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
(i) A cell is a finite set containing $x$ and $C(B)\le C(p,B)+O(1)$.
(ii) A total program knowing $p$ maps $x$ to its cell.
(iii) Follows from (i).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:cells}
For every ambient $G$, up to $O(1)$ shifts in $\alpha$,
\[
  h^G_x=h^{\mathcal{A}_G}_x\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{soph}^G(x)=\mathrm{soph}^{\mathcal{A}_G}(x).
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
A $\mathrm{Par}_G$-model $(p,B)$ has $B\in\mathcal{A}_G$ and $C(B)\le C(p,B)+O(1)$. A set
$B\in\mathcal{A}_G$ containing $x$ gives the $\mathrm{Par}_G$-model $(p_B,B)$ with
$C(p_B,B)\le C(B)+O(1)$. Both by Proposition~\ref{prop:cells}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:dict}
For every ambient $G$, up to $O(1)$ shifts in $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon$,
$h^{L(G)}_x=h^G_x$ and $h^{L(G)}_{x,\varepsilon}=h^G_{x,\varepsilon}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
A pair $(U,U\cdot x)$ gives the $\mathrm{Par}_G$-model $(\mathrm{orb}_G U,U\cdot x)$ at no
greater cost. A $\mathrm{Par}_G$-model $(p,B)$ gives $(\mathrm{stab}_G p,B)$, and
$\mathrm{stab}_G(p)\cdot x=B$ because $p$ is symmetric. Costs are compared by
Proposition~\ref{prop:canon}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:burnside}
If $(p,B)$ is a $\mathrm{Par}_G$-model for $x$ with certificate $U=\mathrm{stab}_G(p)$,
then $|B|=|U|/|\mathrm{stab}_U(x)|=1/\Pr_{u\in U}[ux=x]$, so
$C(x\mid p,B)\le\log|B|+O(1)$. All but a $2^{-t}$ fraction of
$x'\in B$ have $C(x'\mid p,B)\ge\log|B|-t$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:sym}
Up to $O(1)$ shifts, $h^{\mathrm{Sym}}_x=h_x$, so $\mathrm{soph}^{\mathrm{Sym}}=\mathrm{soph}$. Up to
$O(\varepsilon+\log n)$ shifts, $h^{\mathrm{Sym}}_{x,\varepsilon}=h^{\mathrm{str}}_{x,\varepsilon}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Every set is $\mathrm{Sym}$-homogeneous, so the first claim is
Corollary~\ref{cor:cells}; explicitly, for $S\ni x$ the partition
$\{S,X\setminus S\}$ costs $C(S)+O(1)$. For the second claim combine
Proposition~\ref{prop:basicP}(ii) with the partition lemma
(Lemma~\ref{lem:partition}).
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
Up to $O(\varepsilon+\delta+\log n)$, a string is
$(\varepsilon,\delta)$-normal if and only if cells of partitions of
complexity at most $\varepsilon$ (equivalently, orbits of groups of
complexity at most $\varepsilon$) are as good as arbitrary models at
every level. It is strange if and only if no such cell is a minimal
sufficient statistic. So there are strings with no sufficient cheap
symmetry explanation~\cite{V15}, and every admissible shape is realised
by a string whose cheap-symmetry structure function equals its
Kolmogorov structure function~\cite{M16}.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A set $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus\{0\}$ is \emph{linearly homogeneous} if
the relation-preserving permutations of $S$ act transitively on $S$:
for any $s,s'\in S$ some automorphism of the dependency structure maps
$s$ to $s'$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:homog}
Linearly homogeneous sets include: $W\setminus\{0\}$ for a subspace
$W$; affine subspaces $a+W$ with $a\notin W$; linearly independent
sets; weight classes and other orbits of coordinate permutation groups;
and cosets of multiplicative subgroups of $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}^\times$, identifying
$\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$. The set $\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2,e_3\}$ is not
homogeneous: $e_1$ lies in the three-term relation
$\{e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2\}$ while $e_3$ lies in no relation, so no
relation-preserving permutation maps $e_1$ to $e_3$.
Figure~\ref{fig:tess} shows orbits of several subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}(4,2)$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:homog}
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus\{0\}$. Every relation-preserving
permutation of $S$ is the restriction of an element of
$\mathrm{GL}(n,2)_{\{S\}}$. Hence $S$ is $\mathrm{GL}$-homogeneous if and only if it is
linearly homogeneous, and $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GL}}$ consists of $\{0\}$ and the
linearly homogeneous sets. By Corollary~\ref{cor:cells}, $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x$ is
Kolmogorov's structure function restricted to linearly homogeneous sets.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The restriction of a linear map preserves relations. Conversely, a
relation-preserving $\pi$ defines a linear bijection
$L_\pi(\sum_{s\in T}s)=\sum_{s\in T}\pi(s)$ of $\mathrm{span}(S)$. It is
well defined, because $\sum T=\sum T'$ implies $\sum(T\triangle T')=0$
and hence $\sum\pi(T)=\sum\pi(T')$, and it is injective, because
$\pi^{-1}$ also preserves relations. Extending $L_\pi$ by the identity on
a complement of $\mathrm{span}(S)$ gives $g\in\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ with $g(S)=S$
and $g|_S=\pi$. So the restrictions of $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)_{\{S\}}$ to $S$ are
exactly the relation-preserving permutations, and one group is
transitive on $S$ if and only if the other is. Since linear maps fix $0$,
a homogeneous set containing $0$ is $\{0\}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:band}
Let $x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus\{0\}$ with $C(x)=\kappa$. Up to $O(\log n)$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $\kappa-\alpha\le h_x(\alpha)\leh^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(\alpha)\leh^{\mathrm{aff}}_x(\alpha)\le
n-\alpha$ for $c\log n\le\alpha\le\kappa$;
\item $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(c\log n)\le\log(2^n-1)$ and $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(\kappa)=0$;
\item $0\leh^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(\alpha)-h_x(\alpha)\le n-\kappa$, and
$\mathrm{soph}(x)\le\mathrm{soph}^{\mathrm{GL}}(x)\le\kappa$;
\item (relabelling) for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$,
$h^{\mathrm{GL}}_{gx}(\alpha+C(g)+c)\leh^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(\alpha)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
(i) By Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i) and~\eqref{eq:chains}; for the last
inequality use the affine subspace of strings agreeing with $x$ in the
first $j$ coordinates. (ii) Use the partitions $\{\{0\},\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus\{0\}\}$
and the discrete partition. (iii) Follows from (i) and (ii). (iv) By
equivariance of the Galois connection.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{q:accept}
Is $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GL}}$ acceptable, i.e.\ can every $S\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GL}}$ of size $N$
be covered by $\mathrm{poly}(n)\,N/c$ members of $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{GL}}$ of size at
most $c$? In the language of Section~\ref{sec:algebra}: does every
cell admit cheap symmetric refinements, for instance by meets? If not,
does $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x$ exhibit a plateau for some $x$?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:zerogap}
For every admissible shape $P$ there is a string $x$ with
$h_x\approxh^{\mathrm{GL}}_x\approxh^{\mathrm{aff}}_x\approx P$, up to
$C(P)+O(\sqrt{n\log n})$, so $\mathrm{soph}^{\mathrm{GL}}(x)=\mathrm{soph}(x)$ to the same
accuracy.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:VV} applied to affine subspaces, and~\eqref{eq:chains}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:maxgap}
There is a constant $c$ such that for all $n$, all $c\log n\le m\le n$
and all $t\ge0$ there are strings $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ with:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
\item $C(x)=m\pm O(t+\log n)$ and $h_x(\alpha)=m-\alpha\pm O(t+\log n)$ for
$c\log n\le\alpha\le m$; $x$ is stochastic and
$(O(\log n),O(t+\log n))$-normal;
\item $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(\alpha)\ge n-\alpha-t-O(\log n)$ for all
$\alpha\le m-t-c\log n$.
\end{enumerate}
In fact all but a $2^{-t}$ fraction of a set $S$ with $C(S)=O(\log n)$
and $|S|\approx2^m$ have these properties.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
\emph{Counting cells.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:GLtype}, or simply
because a group of order $N$ has a generating set of size $\log N$, there
are at most $2^{n^4}$ subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$, hence at most $2^{n^4+n}$
cells of symmetric partitions.

\emph{A set that no cell sees.} Put each string into a random $S$
independently with probability $2^{m-n}$. For a cell $B$ let
$R_B=\max(2e\,2^{m-n}|B|,n^5)$. The Chernoff bound
$\Pr[X\ge R]\le2^{-R}$ for $R\ge2e\,\mathbb{E}X$~\cite{MU} gives
$\Pr[|S\cap B|\ge R_B]\le2^{-n^5}$. A union bound, and concentration of
$|S|$, show that with positive probability
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pi}
2^{m-1}\le|S|\le2^{m+1}\quad\text{and}\quad
|S\cap B|<\max(2e\,2^{m-n}|B|,\,n^5)\ \text{for every cell }B.
\end{equation}
This property is decidable, so the lexicographically first such $S$ has
$C(S)=O(\log n)$.

\emph{Typical elements.} All but a $2^{-t}$ fraction of $x\in S$ have
$C(x)\ge m-t$; fix one.

(a) Cutting $S$ into $2^j$ consecutive pieces gives models of complexity
$j+O(\log n)$ and size at most $2^{m+1-j}$, each computable from $x$ by a
total program of length $O(\log n)$. With Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}(i) this
gives $h_x$ and normality.

(b) Fix $\alpha,s$. Fewer than $2^{\alpha+1}$ models $(p,B)$ have
$C(p,B)\le\alpha$, and the union $U$ of those cells with $|B|\le2^s$ is
enumerable from $n,m,\alpha,s$. By~\eqref{eq:pi},
$|U\cap S|\le2^{\alpha+1}\max(2e\,2^{m-n+s},n^5)$. If $x\in U$, then
\[
  m-t\le C(x)\le\log|U\cap S|+O(\log n)
  \le\alpha+\max(m-n+s,\ 5\log n)+O(\log n).
\]
For $\alpha\le m-t-c\log n$ the second branch is impossible, so
$s\ge n-\alpha-t-O(\log n)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:sep}
If moreover $m\le n-t-c'\log n$, these strings satisfy
$\mathrm{soph}(x)=O(\log n)$ but $\mathrm{soph}^{\mathrm{GL}}(x)\ge C(x)-O(t+\log n)$. They are
stochastic and normal, yet no cell of a symmetric partition costing
less than $C(x)-O(t+\log n)$ is sufficient: every sufficient symmetric
model essentially names $x$ itself. The gap between the two chains
in~\eqref{eq:chains} is a symmetry phenomenon, not a computability one.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By (b), $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x(\alpha)+\alpha\ge n-t-O(\log n)>C(x)+c\log n$ for
$\alpha\le m-t-c\log n$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The argument only uses that the partition family has
$2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ cells and is decidable. So every such family,
for instance $\mathrm{Par}_G$ for any ambient group of order $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$,
has stochastic normal strings that it sees as antistochastic. The
construction is not explicit.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Let $B_N(H)$ be the set of faithful $b=\sum a_i[H/K_i]$ of degree $N$.
Fix $H$ concretely (with a total order on its elements) and the
representatives $K_i$ canonically. For $b\in B_N(H)$ let $X_b$ be the
disjoint union of $a_i$ copies of $H/K_i$, ordered by $i$, then by copy,
then by the least element of each coset. Identify $X_b$ with $X$ in
lexicographic order. This gives a faithful action $\rho_b$ and a
\emph{canonical subgroup} $U_b=\rho_b(H)\le S_X$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:coords}
Let $\mathcal S_H(X)=\{U\le S_X : U\cong H\}$ and
\[
  \Phi_H\colon B_N(H)\times S_X\to\mathcal S_H(X),\qquad
  \Phi_H(b,\sigma)=\sigma\,U_b\,\sigma^{-1}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $\Phi_H$ is surjective: every $U\cong H$ has coordinates $(b,\sigma)$.
\item For fixed $b$, $\Phi_H(b,\sigma)=\Phi_H(b,\sigma')$ iff
$\sigma^{-1}\sigma'\in N_{S_X}(U_b)$.
\item $\Phi_H(b,\sigma)$ and $\Phi_H(b',\sigma')$ are conjugate in $S_X$
iff $b'\in\mathrm{Aut}(H)\cdot b$, where $\alpha\in\mathrm{Aut}(H)$ acts by
$[H/K]\mapsto[H/\alpha(K)]$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently
\[
  \mathcal S_H(X)\;=\;\bigsqcup_{[b]\in B_N(H)/\mathrm{Aut}(H)}
  S_X/N_{S_X}(U_b):
\]
the \emph{type} $[b]$ is a discrete coordinate labelling conjugacy
classes, and the \emph{placement} $\sigma$ is a coordinate on the
homogeneous space $S_X/N_{S_X}(U_b)$. The whole space of permutation
groups on $X$ is the disjoint union of these pieces over the isomorphism
classes of $H$ with a faithful action of degree $N$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(i) Fix an isomorphism $\psi\colon H\to U$. The $H$-set $X$ with action
$\psi$ is faithful of some class $b\in B_N(H)$, so there is an
isomorphism of $H$-sets $\sigma\colon(X,\rho_b)\to(X,\psi)$, i.e.
$\sigma\rho_b(h)\sigma^{-1}=\psi(h)$ for all $h$. Hence
$U=\sigma U_b\sigma^{-1}$. (ii) This is the definition of the
normaliser. (iii) If $\tau U_b\tau^{-1}=U_{b'}$, then
$\alpha=\rho_{b'}^{-1}\circ c_\tau\circ\rho_b$ is an automorphism of $H$,
and $\tau$ is an isomorphism of $H$-sets from $X_b$ to $X_{b'}$ twisted
by $\alpha$, so $b'=\alpha\cdot b$. The converse reverses the argument.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:coordcost}
Let $U=\Phi_H(b,\sigma)$, with $b$ chosen canonically in its
$\mathrm{Aut}(H)$-orbit. Then, up to $O(\log C(U))$,
\[
  C(U)\;=\;C(H,b)\;+\;\min\{\,C(\sigma'\mid H,b) : \Phi_H(b,\sigma')=U\,\}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
From $U$ one computes $H$ up to isomorphism, the canonical $b$, and the
least $\sigma$ in the coset $\sigma N_{S_X}(U_b)$. This least element is
computable from any member of the coset together with $(H,b)$. Apply
symmetry of information.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
For subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ the same construction applies with $B(H)$
replaced by the isomorphism classes of faithful $\mathbb{F}_2H$-modules of
dimension $n$ (the Green ring), and $S_X$ by $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$. The fibres are
then $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)/N_{\mathrm{GL}(n,2)}(U_b)$, and the placement costs at most $n^2$
bits (Proposition~\ref{prop:GLtype}).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:placement}
Let $S\subseteq X$, and let $p$ be any partition of $X$ having $S$ as a
cell (by Example~\ref{ex:cells}(a) there are many, the coarsest being
$\{S,X\setminus S\}$), with canonical certificate $U=\mathrm{stab}_{S_X}(p)$. Let $\lambda(p)$ be
the multiset of cell sizes of $p$, an integer partition of $N=2^n$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $U=\prod_{B\in p}\mathrm{Sym}(B)$ is a Young subgroup, and its type
$(H,b)$ is determined by $\lambda(p)$: $H=\prod_{B\in p}S_{|B|}$, and $b$
has one orbit of type $H/H_B$ for each cell $B$, where $H_B$ is the
stabiliser of a point of $B$. Hence
\[
  C(H,b)\le C(\lambda(p))+O(1)\le\log P(N)+O(n)=O(2^{n/2}),
\]
where $P(N)$ is the number of integer partitions of $N$.
\item Every placement realising $U$ is expensive:
\[
  \min\{C(\sigma\mid H,b) : \Phi_H(b,\sigma)=U\}\ \ge\
  C(S)-C(\lambda(p))-O(n).
\]
In particular the placement carries at least $C(S)-O(2^{n/2})$ bits,
for every partition realising $S$.
\item For $p=\{S\}\cup\{\text{singletons}\}$ with $|S|=k\ge2$, the type
is $H=S_k$, $b=[S_k/S_{k-1}]+(2^n-k)[S_k/S_k]$, costing $O(n)$, and the
placement costs $C(S)\pm O(n)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
(i) By Example~\ref{ex:closed}(a) the closed subgroups of $S_X$ are the
Young subgroups. A Young subgroup is determined up to conjugacy by its
cell sizes, and its abstract group and Burnside ring element are
computable from them. Given $N$, the partition $\lambda(p)$ is one of
$P(N)$ possibilities, and by the Hardy--Ramanujan formula
$\log_2P(N)\sim\pi\sqrt{2N/3}/\ln2=O(2^{n/2})$.
(ii) Since $U\le S_X$, $C(U)\le n2^n+O(1)$, so the error term in
Proposition~\ref{prop:coordcost} is $O(n)$. From $U$ one computes $p$,
and $S$ is one of at most $N$ cells of $p$. Hence
$C(S)\le C(H,b)+\min C(\sigma\mid H,b)+n+O(n)$; now use (i).
(iii) $S$ is the unique cell of size greater than one, so
$C(U)=C(S)\pm O(1)$, and the type is described by $k$ and $n$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The type is cheap, but it is not empty. Write $b=\sum_i a_i[H/K_i]$. For
any ambient group, the cells of $\Phi_H(b,\sigma)$ have sizes
$|H:K_i|$ with multiplicities $a_i$, and there are $\sum_i a_i$ of them.
In the three-part description~\eqref{eq:threepart} this divides the
terms between the coordinates:
\[
  C(x)\ \lesssim\
  \underbrace{C(H,b)+C(\sigma\mid H,b)}_{\text{hypothesis, }C(p)}
  \ +\ \underbrace{\log\textstyle\sum_i a_i}_{\text{which cell}}
  \ +\ \underbrace{\log|H:K_i|}_{\text{noise}},
\]
where $i$ is the orbit type of the cell containing $x$. Both
data-to-model terms are read off from the type: it fixes how many cells
there are and the multiset of their sizes, and so locates every cell on
the vertical axis of the structure function. It does not fix the size
of the cell containing $x$, which depends on the placement, unless all
cells have the same size, as for free or transitive actions. For $S_X$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:placement} shows that the division is nearly
clean: the type costs $O(2^{n/2})$ bits and carries the sizes, while the
placement carries essentially all of $C(p)$. A Young subgroup says how
large the cells are, and nothing about which sets they are. For
$\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ the two do not separate in this way, since the type
determines the hypothesis up to $n^2$ bits
(Proposition~\ref{prop:GLtype}).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:weight}
Let $p_{\mathrm{wt}}$ be the partition of $\{0,1\}^n$ into weight
classes. It is the orbit partition of the coordinate group $S_n$
permuting bit positions, a small group with structured type
$\sum_{w=0}^n[S_n/(S_w\times S_{n-w})]$. It is also the orbit partition
of the Young subgroup $\prod_w\mathrm{Sym}(\{x:|x|=w\})$, whose type is just the
list of binomial coefficients $\binom nw$. Both certify the same
hypothesis at the same canonical cost $O(\log n)$. With ambient group
$S_X$, however, the Galois connection selects the Young subgroup, so the
canonical certificate forgets the symmetry that actually explains the
partition. With ambient group $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ the closed subgroup of
$p_{\mathrm{wt}}$ is exactly the group of permutation matrices, since a
linear map preserving weight sends each $e_i$ to some $e_j$. There the
certificate keeps its structure. Figure~\ref{fig:s8types} shows types and
placements in $S_X$ for $n=3$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:GLtype}
Let $U\le\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ have coordinates $(b,g)$ as in the remark at the end of
Section~\ref{sec:coordthm}: $b$ is the class of a faithful
$\mathbb{F}_2H$-module of dimension $n$ and $g\in\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ is a placement. Then,
up to $O(\log n)$,
\[
  C(H,b)\ \le\ C(U)\ \le\ C(H,b)+n^2 .
\]
Consequently the number of symmetric partitions in $\mathrm{Par}_{\mathrm{GL}}$ is
at most the number of types times $|\mathrm{GL}(n,2)|$, which is less than
$2^{n^2}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The type is computable from $U$. Conversely $U=gU_bg^{-1}$, where $U_b$
is computable from the type and $g$ is an $n\times n$ matrix.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{q:rigid}
Is there a string $x$ for which $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_x$ and $h^{\mathrm{str}}_{x,\varepsilon}$ are
both small at some level, yet $h^{\mathrm{GL}}_{x,\varepsilon}$ is large there?
Such an $x$ would have a good linearly homogeneous model and a good
strong model, but no cheap symmetric partition, a separation caused
by the rigidity of $\mathrm{Par}_{\mathrm{GL}}$ rather than by computability.
<!-- end question-2 -->
